https://www.politico.eu/article/why-the-.text: STOCKHOLM — As far-right leader Jimmie Åkesson danced beside the pink balaclava-wearing singer Miss Smut at his final campaign rally, he hoped a late surge in the polls would carry his Sweden Democrats into power. But the following day’s election instead delivered a rude shock to Sweden’s anti-immigration vanguard: A loss of vote share, support and influence for the first time since the SD was founded by neo-Nazis in the 1980s. The left bloc narrowly won the contest and will now seek to form a government that doesn’t include any right-wing parties. Advertisement Advertisement Amid reports of recriminations within the SD, Åkesson may take time away from frontline politics, but insists he won’t resign. Jimmie Åkesson’s final rally takes place in Stockholm on Sept. 12, 2026. | Tim Ross/POLITICO The disappointing outcome for the SD is a rarity these days in European politics: A far-right populist party making a name for itself campaigning against immigration, but then falling back instead of grasping power. POLITICO spoke to experts and key players, including outgoing center-right Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson and his likely Social Democrat replacement Magdalena Andersson, to draw some lessons from the campaign. The far right allied with the center — and lost The SD’s vote share fell from 20.5% in 2022 to 17.5% this year, even though it had supported Kristersson’s center-right coalition within the parliament for four years. Although Åkesson’s party succeeded in pushing Kristersson’s administration to adopt tougher policies on crime and immigration, their electoral result was ultimately worse. Kristersson’s Moderates party, meanwhile, increased its support and overtook the SD to become the second-largest force in the parliament. That outcome will have drawn the notice of German Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats and the far-right Alternative for Germany, for example, as well as of Britain’s Conservative Party and Reform UK. It’s OK to blame voters, if it fits your story Åkesson’s explanation for the SD’s disappointing result was bang on brand for an anti-migrant populist. At a Friday press conference he claimed the Social Democrats and their allies on the left had been “very good at mobilizing the Islamist voters who previously had other parties to vote for.” Advertisement Advertisement At the same time, he said, some right-wing supporters had voted for tiny parties that didn’t make it over the 4% vote threshold required for representation in parliament. Åkesson wasn’t alone in flagging voter behavior. Social Democrat leader Andersson spent much of the campaign warning voters not to put Åkesson and his team in power, casting it as a central election issue. She told POLITICO on election day that voters who supported Kristersson and other right-wing parties, knowing that support would put far-right ministers in government for the first time, were “in denial.” “They don’t really want to see that they actually vote for a government dominated by Sweden Democrats,” she said. Swedish firewall held, but more by chance than design Mainstream European parties have for decades pursued a “firewall” policy against the far right to block it from power, determined to prevent a return of the fascism that so scarred Europe in the 20th century. In reality, Sweden formerly stout firewall has developed many holes over the past four years. Kristersson broke the taboo against working with the SD back in 2022 when, in a coalition with two other right-wing parties, he signed a deal to implement key SD priorities in exchange for their support in parliament. The pact gave Åkesson significant influence over Kristersson’s government, allowing the SD to drive a hardline crackdown on immigration and an agenda to tackle violent crime. Advertisement Advertisement Sweden’s Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson, leader of the conservative Moderates, speaks to the press during the Moderates’ election night party in Stockholm in the early hours of September 14, 2026. | Christine Olsson/AFP via Getty Images Kristersson dismissed criticism that he was opening the door to extremists who would end Sweden as a tolerant country. Billing himself as a pragmatist, he asked voters to judge him on his government’s success at bringing down crime and immigration. “For me, it’s the result that counts,” Kristersson told POLITICO in the final week of the campaign. In order to solve problems, he said, you need a majority in the parliament — which under Sweden’s proportional representation system meant working with the SD. Don’t take normalization too far Ahead of the election Kristersson went a step further, for the first time promising Åkesson seats in his Cabinet if their rightwing alliance retained power. “That probably was beyond the pale for a small number of people who would otherwise have voted for one of the right-wing parties, particularly the Liberals,” said Nicholas Aylott, associate professor of politics at Södertörn University. In a close election, he said, such small things can make a big difference. Overall, Aylott said, the firewall wasn’t central to this year’s election, despite attempts by left-wing parties to make it so. Whatever the impact of Kristersson’s gambit, this election was almost a tie and nearly went the other way. If two seats had flipped to the right bloc, Åkesson’s team would be preparing to take over key ministries in the government. And if Andersson can’t persuade other parties to back her in coalition talks, that could still happen. Advertisement Advertisement Firewalls don’t work forever The Sweden Democrats entered parliament for the first time in 2010 — and mainstream center and left-wing parties refused to cooperate with them. According to Aylott, that “very strong” firewall allowed the SD to build support in the country. “That created a huge space in the Swedish political context in which anyone with any sort of cautious or skeptical view toward immigration at the time really had only the Sweden Democrats to choose,” he said. By 2022, with gang crime rife, the SD’s tough stance on law and order and migration drove it to its best-ever result. Its second-place finish put in a powerful position to influence Kristersson’s government. It’s not a coincidence, Aylott said, that the far right fell back again after the firewall was partly set aside to allow it to join the government, for all that it didn’t have ministers in Kristersson’s Cabinet. The firewall “is not holding anymore” in much of Europe, according to Grégoire Roos, Europe program director at the Chatham House think tank in London. “The citizens who cast their ballots for these parties are increasingly young. So referring to the darkest times of history does not appeal to them at all,” Roos said. “To some extent, the more you bash these parties, the more popular they get,” he added, noting it was true of Trump and others in Europe. “I think in this regard we can see a pattern.” Advertisement Advertisement Normal for Nordics It’s not unusual for the far right to be integrated into governments in Nordic countries such as Norway and Finland. The center left in Denmark has also adopted particularly tough policies against migration, in part to mitigate the appeal of far-right populists. These recent developments contrast sharply with the situation in Southern and Western European countries like Germany, Spain and France. Pro-Russian policies cost you votes While some European far-right parties have maintained pro-Russia attitudes without incurring major electoral costs, that’s not the case in countries like Sweden. Sweden’s authorities regard Russia as the country’s No. 1 security threat, while Moscow has menaced Swedish airspace and interests in the Baltic Sea in recent years. Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022 prompted Sweden to end decades of military neutrality and join NATO — a decision that has enjoyed wide public and political support. In the final days of the election campaign, the SD was hit by a scandal over alleged Russian infiltration — an inevitable voter repellent in Swedish politics. Immigration isn’t the issue it used to be After Sweden’s record 2015 intake of asylum seekers, the political backlash saw governments of both persuasions introduce harsh restrictions — reducing migrant numbers by 96% a decade later. Advertisement Andersson, who also favors limits on immigration, said some of the governing coalition’s policies had gone too far for average Swedes, such as deporting the teenage children of migrants who had grown up in Sweden. “These are young people that are part of the club and now they have to leave,” she said. “People don’t like it.” Far right a victim of its own success Two big issues that had driven support for the SD in previous elections — gang shootings and immigration — were lower on the agenda in this election, Aylott said. Perhaps because Kristersson’s coalition, with the SD’s support, had succeeded in reducing gun crime and throttling immigration. Four years ago, the headlines were all about “gang violence, daily shootings, kids being killed,” Kristersson told POLITICO. “Now we have brought that down by some 80%.” On immigration, Kristersson’s government began paying some foreign-born people €30,000 to leave the country. “For me, results matter,” Kristersson said. His Moderates party won more seats this time around — perhaps a sign of voter gratitude — but the SD, which was so closely identified with anti-immigration policies, fell back. “The paradox is that when the situation begins to feel less acute, it falls down the list of voters’ priorities,” said Aylott. When that happens, “probably the party that was favored is not going to be favored again.” Advertisement Healthcare, education and the economy topped the list of voter concerns, according to exit polls . Centrist governments should just do their jobs Andersson believes the SD can be fought on their traditional right-wing economic positions as well as on “the hate they have spread” and would propagate further if they won office. Above all, she said, the lesson for centrists is that they have to deliver on voters’ concerns when they have the chance. Magdalena Andersson and her husband Richard Friberg greet elderly people as they arrive to cast their vote at a polling station in a school during Sweden’s general election, in Nacka on September 13, 2026. | Jonathan Nackstrand/ AFP via Getty Images “If you have governments that actually do deliver better living standards, better schools, better healthcare, build a society where people can feel hope for the future, then the room for right-wing populist parties will be smaller,” she said. “It’s clear that after the financial crisis of 2008- 2009, traditional parties haven’t really been able to deliver.” Even Kristersson, although his bloc lost power, saw his center-right Moderates increase their share of the vote after a campaign in which he highlighted his government’s successes. Far right not dead yet Andersson said support for the far right “is not something you stop in a four-year period.” Voters across Europe choose populist nationalist parties “because politics is not delivering,” she told POLITICO. Advertisement “If traditional political parties aren’t delivering a better hope for a better future, then you vote for something else. So it’s really up to us to do our homework: Deliver when we are in power, and in opposition have good and realistic programs that we can deliver on once we are in power again.” Aylott agreed that while the election was “certainly a setback” for the SD, it wasn’t a “total collapse.” There has been speculation that Åkesson could walk away from the SD in the weeks ahead. If that happens, a new leader could revive the party with a return to a more radical posture, Aylott said. The freedom to speak out that comes with being in opposition will also likely help. “It’s not inconceivable that we might see some re-radicalization of the party and an attempt to fire up the activists again,” Aylott said. “This could be a critical moment for the party. It could lead to infighting and very damaging disputes, but it could equally lead to a sort of renewal of the party’s appeal, perhaps with a younger leader.”

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: Student protesters in the Place de la Bastille in Paris, 8 October 2026 Photograph: Orin Louis/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock View image in fullscreen Student protesters in the Place de la Bastille in Paris, 8 October 2026 Photograph: Orin Louis/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock Opinion France Angry French students take to the streets. British students don’t – and I think I know why Kitty Sayers I grew up in France, where all children are taught about the revolutionary roots of their nation and what the state owes its citizens. The lessons leave their mark Sat 10 Oct 2026 05.45 EDT First published on Sat 10 Oct 2026 05.00 EDT Share Y oung British people have plenty to be angry about. Crushing student debt, private-school privilege, a housing market they can’t enter. Yet unlike their French counterparts, they have little tradition of turning that frustration into collective action. I grew up in France as a Briton, and for years I have watched my French friends do something my British ones never seem to: take to the streets. “To arms, citizens! Form your battalions! Let’s march, let’s march!” It shouldn’t be too surprising, given the rousing lyrics of La Marseillaise, that France’s revolutionary spirit is not a relic of the past. The lycée protests in the past week have displayed the organisation and bravery of the French students. In Lens, a 15-year-old lost his hand to a police grenade during a blockade. More than 6,000 people have been arrested , many of them under 18. Hundreds of schools across France are either blockaded or closed. These teenagers know the risks and commit to turning up anyway, day after day. I can’t imagine that happening in Britain, so what makes the French so different? First, there’s the history. France’s republic was born of insurrection and has never forgotten it. French pupils learn that protest, uprising and rioting are the origin story of their freedoms, so these methods are championed in promoting change. We grew up in school with the idea that if you don’t like something, you have the power to change it. The language of rights, citizenship and collective power is woven into French education. The French Revolution appears in the curriculum twice, for pupils aged 12 and then again at 16; the student protests of 1968 are taught at age 14 and again at 17. Debating is encouraged in schools from as early as collège , or at about 11 years old. Young people are expected to have an opinion and not be afraid to defend it. Even I, at 11, started to feel patriotic during our moral and civic education classes, despite not having a French passport. Protesting is taught as a legally framed fundamental right and a civic responsibility. Of course, with lycéens not yet being old enough to vote, protest is the next best thing. In the final year of lycée , pupils study Rousseau’s Du Contrat Social (The Social Contract), which argues that citizens should only surrender their unrestricted natural liberty in exchange for civil and moral freedoms. You give up your individual interests for the volonté générale (general will) – put simply, you pay heavy taxes and in return you expect the country to work. That bargain is how the French understand their relationship with the state. When the government raises the retirement age, lets electricity bills soar or cuts school budgets, that is seen as a breach of the social contract. Protest is the automatic response. Britons, on the other hand, are subjects of the UK and are characterised more by an American-style individualism and a desire to live and let live. There is less collective spirit . Britain has an extraordinary history of protest, spanning Peterloo, the Chartists, the suffragettes and the poll tax riots, but there is arguably a different cultural relationship to these events. They can be remembered as stand-alone episodes and interruptions to the national story rather than as the story itself. The Thatcher era also did permanent damage to unions, contributing to the British public being a grumbling but compliant one, lacking in organising power. I see what’s happening here in Paris: reasonable student demands met with awful violence | Helen Massy-Beresford Read more Because these values are ingrained across French society, and in every generation, the student protesters are emboldened by the firefighters, nurses, lawyers and teachers who have joined them in solidarity. Across social media, you can see these moments of support and unity. A viral video of the mayor of Saint-Denis, Bally Bagayoko , protecting students from the police is a striking example of this. It’s difficult to imagine British teenagers taking to the streets, because they would be alone. Parents have joined their children in protesting, and have called on other parents to do the same for the planned general strike on 17 October. (This is also a response to the police brutality witnessed in the past week.) Many parents were themselves lycée students and marched against education reforms and cuts. The anti-Macroniste parents (of whom there are many) don’t treat their children as delinquents, but as citizens exercising their rights. That does not mean every French parent supports every protest, or that French society is wholly united behind its students. While the French state technically encourages protest through the curriculum, the force and violence with which it has met its students says otherwise. And there is resentment of the protests among some students, particularly those who come from conservative households and believe that the blockades are a leftwing plot. Students in France are not necessarily more political than their British counterparts – young British people are active, but tend to take part in established and larger movements such as Extinction Rebellion or the Gaza protests rather than initiate protests themselves. The biggest difference lies in the French willingness to take to the streets, suddenly and en-masse. Unlike in the UK, the state is something the French are taught to engage with as citizens, and to challenge when necessary. If anything, the lycéens are just being good students. Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Facebook Twitter WhatsApp SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Internal medicine physician Anna Mehlich, M.D., has joined the caregivers at Winona Health and is now seeing patients in internal medicine. Originally from Opole, Poland, Dr. Mehlich speaks both English and Polish and is excited to become part of the Winona community. Dr. Mehlich provides comprehensive primary care for adults, with particular interests in diabetes management, healthy weight management, preventive care, and helping patients make lasting lifestyle changes that support overall health and wellness. "I strongly believe that primary care is one of the most important parts of health care," said Dr. Mehlich. "We have the opportunity to focus on prevention, education, and screening, helping patients avoid serious illnesses before they develop. Building those long-term relationships and helping people stay healthy is what drew me to this work." Dr. Mehlich describes her approach to care as a combination of knowledge, compassion, and humility. "Patients come to us because they need help, and it's our responsibility to have the knowledge to provide the care they deserve," she said. "But knowledge alone isn't enough. Every patient is a person who may be facing fears, stress, financial concerns, or challenges we don't immediately see. Taking the time to listen and understand their story helps build trust and allows us to provide better care." She also believes in being open and honest with patients. "There is no way any physician can know everything," Dr. Mehlich said. "It's important to keep an open mind and be willing to say, 'I don't know, but I will find the answer and get back to you.' Patients deserve that honesty." Dr. Mehlich discovered her interest in medicine as a teenager while volunteering with older adults in her community. "I always wanted to do something meaningful with my life," she said. "Spending time with people who were facing health challenges inspired me. I realized how valuable it is to help others and to understand what they were experiencing from a medical perspective." Dr. Mehlich earned her medical degree from the Medical University of Warsaw in Poland and completed her internal medicine residency at John H. Stroger Jr. Hospital of Cook County in Chicago, where she cared for patients with a wide range of complex medical needs. During residency, she received the Resident Humanitarian Award, recognizing her compassion for patients and commitment to exceptional care. She was drawn to Winona Health because of its strong commitment to patients and the community. "From my first visit, I felt welcomed," she said. "There was a warmth here that stood out to me. Winona Health feels like a place where people genuinely care about each other, and I am excited to become part of this community." In her free time, Dr. Mehlich enjoys cooking, baking, hiking, and following sports. She and her husband, who is completing fellowship training, enjoy spending time with their three-year-old daughter and exploring Winona, their new community. To learn more about Dr. Mehlich, including additional provider information and fun facts, visit winonahealth.org , and search “Find a Provider.” To schedule an appointment with Dr. Mehlich in internal medicine, call 507-457-7622. Photograph: Rocco Fazzari/AAP Sydney Beau Lamarre-Condon denies making fake Grindr account for Jesse Baird, double murder trial hears Former police officer accused of murdering Baird and Luke Davies cross-examined in NSW supreme court Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Kat Wong Tue 10 Nov 2026 21.44 EST First published on Tue 10 Nov 2026 20.00 EST Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Beau Lamarre-Condon has denied making a fake dating app account of Jesse Baird after their breakup, a court has heard. The former police officer is accused of fatally shooting Baird and his new partner, Luke Davies, with his police service weapon in Baird’s Paddington home in Sydney on 19 February 2024. He has pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter. Earlier during his double murder trial at the New South Wales supreme court, a friend of Lamarre-Condon’s gave evidence that he had made fake profiles of Baird on apps like Grindr. Sitting in the witness box for the fifth day, Lamarre-Condon was asked whether he told a friend he had made a fake Grindr account in relation to Baird, after one of the former officer’s friends earlier gave evidence about the matter. Under cross-examination from crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC on Wednesday, Lamarre-Condon said that had “never happened”. Lamarre-Condon told the court that after his breakup with Baird, he had tried to create a fake account for a man the presenter had been seeing. “I attempted to create a fake account with an email I believed was from him to see if it was active … to see if he was in an exclusive relationship with Jesse or not,” he said. “But I didn’t make an account or operate it as him.” He claimed he was only seeing whether that address was available on the app as it would indicate whether or not he was using the service. Hatfield suggested the email he had entered was not that man’s address and asked whether Lamarre-Condon had created it himself. The former policeman responded: “I can’t confirm if this is 100% [his] email or not, this is something I had seen on social media.” ‘I definitely didn’t manufacture a bump-in’ In August 2023, while Lamarre-Condon and Baird were still broken up, the former officer allegedly broke into Baird’s home and attempted to go through his phone. The court previously heard Lamarre-Condon accidentally woke Baird up while using his phone and was chased out of the house by the other man. On Wednesday, Hatfield asked whether the former officer “manufactured” an opportunity to bump into Baird after the alleged break-in to “sus out whether he suspected it was you or not”. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion Lamarre-Condon responded: “I definitely didn’t manufacture a bump-in”, telling the court he made plans with Baird to meet him in the coming days. Asked by the prosecution if he was going to tell Baird it was him who entered the home, Lamarre-Condon said: “Yes and he didn’t ask me”. Hatfield then asked Lamarre-Condon if he had turned his phone to airplane mode for an hour on the night of the alleged break-in. He agreed, but repeated that he entered the terrace house with a key that had been left out for him. A few weeks later, Lamarre-Condon met with Baird on the presenter’s birthday. That night, the former officer texted a friend, telling her: “He rejected my kiss”. Hatfield asked: “Is it the case the reason why you’re sending the text … is that he rejected your kiss and that’s what happened?” But Lamarre-Condon denied this, saying: “no that’s not correct that was at the start … we definitely did hook up on this night”. The trial before Justice Natalie Adams continues.
